line: A warm year. This year favours early-run fish. Late-run fish burn more fat on the way home.
High water. This year, early-run and deep-bodied fish struggle more against the flow.
Low water. This year, deep-bodied fish are easier for bears to reach in the shallows.
A big run. More big males crowd the spawning grounds: harder for large males, more fights and openings for jacks.
A small run. Fewer rivals on the spawning grounds, which suits large males and leaves jacks fewer openings.
A crowded ocean. Fish grow less at sea and come home smaller.
An ordinary year. No trait has a clear advantage.
Every year favours different fish. Over many years, a population that keeps its variety does better than one that bets on a single strategy.

Each panel shows the inherited part of a trait, averaged over the brood each fish was chosen from. Zero is the home population's average. The offspring you pick, the mates they meet, strays and chance all move it.
The whole brood died before any of them could spawn. Nothing of this line returns to the gravel.
Salmon sometimes stray from the stream they were born in. A stray that has joined this river can start a new line here.
A cool year. This year favours late-run fish, which burn less fat on the way home.

when: At the start of the stage
line: An egg in the gravel. There is little an egg can do but wait. Cold water seeps between the stones.
Hatched. The alevin lives on its yolk sac, hidden in the gravel. Alevin turn to face into the current: it keeps them upright and keeps oxygen-rich water flowing over their gills.
The flow is shifting. Turn to face into the current before it surges.
The current is working you loose. Face upstream and sink deeper into the gravel.
The yolk is nearly gone. Swim up toward the light and out of the gravel, ready to feed.

when: At the end of the stage
line: The fry wriggles up out of the stones and into open water. Only about 10 to 20 percent of eggs get this far.
Not yet. Higher in the gravel the surges hit harder. Rise when the yolk is nearly used.

when: At the start of the stage
line: The lake. Most sockeye spend one year here, some two, feeding on zooplankton.

when: At the start, first life only
line: Click the water to steer with the mouse. Swim forward, burst, rise and dive. Swim through the glowing plankton to feed.
A Dolly Varden has seen you. Rings in the water warn of a chase. The weeds at the shallow edge give cover.
Hidden in the weeds. The Dolly Varden loses interest.

when: At the end of the stage
line: Winter comes. Under the ice the fry grows slowly. Only about 5 to 10 percent of fry survive to leave the lake.
Early summer, at the weed edge. Watch for rings spreading through the water: they mean a Dolly Varden is about to chase. When you see them, dart into the weeds.
Well read. Food in the open is worth having, but only with cover close by.
Midsummer evenings. As the light fades, the plankton rises toward the surface. The richest feeding is up high, in open water, where Dolly Varden and trout hunt.
The water is cold and food is scarce. Every burst spends reserves you cannot easily replace. Rest when you can: ease off and take only the food that drifts close.
The reserves are gone, and the fry is burning its own growth to stay alive. Rest, and find food.
Spring. The ice breaks up.

About 6 in 10 sockeye leave the lake after one year. Follow the drifting current to the outlet to leave now, or wait in the weeds to stay another year: a bigger fish when it leaves, but another year among the predators.
This fry grew well this year.
This fry grew slowly this year. Another year in the lake would make it bigger when it leaves.
Staying another year.
A second summer in the lake.
Bigger now, but the predators are still here. Feed at dusk, and keep the weeds close.
Another winter passes under the ice.
After one year in the lake, like most sockeye, the young fish follows the current toward the outlet.
After two years in the lake, a bigger young fish follows the current toward the outlet.

when: At the start of the stage
line: Spring. The young fish turns silver and leaves the lake at night, with thousands of others. Going together swamps the predators: they cannot eat everyone. Stay with the school.
Char wait at the lake outlet. Rings in the water warn of a lunge. In a school, the char may take another fish instead of you.
A shadow on the surface: a diving bird. Go deep, or hide under the overhanging banks.
A splash ahead: a merganser diving. It will chase underwater for a few seconds. Burst away.
The river mouth and the first salt water. Gulls gather overhead and seals hunt the channel.
Gulls, several at once. Watch every shadow.
Bubbles and a dark shape in the deep water: a seal. It will lunge straight. Swim across its path.
You've left the school. A lone fish is the predators' only choice.

file: (not recorded: contains a number that changes)
when: At the end of the stage
line: The estuary. Of the {total} smolts that left the lake beside you, {lost} were taken. Since it turned silver, its gills and kidneys have been readying it for salt water.

when: At the start of the stage
line: The North Pacific. Sockeye stay in the top 20 to 40 metres and do most of their growing here. Feed where the krill and small fish gather.
A dark shape at the edge of sight: an orca. It will charge in a straight line. Swim across its path, not away from it.
The orca is gone.

Something has changed. This male is maturing early, after a single year at sea. He will return small, about 300 millimetres: a jack. Jacks are rare: in a typical Bristol Bay run only 1 or 2 males in 100 do this.
2 years at sea in all. This male will return large, with a hooked jaw, big teeth and a hump.
3 years at sea in all. This male will return large, with a hooked jaw, big teeth and a hump.
After 2 years at sea, she turns for home.
After 3 years at sea, she turns for home.
A fast grey shape below: a salmon shark. It will strike in a straight line. Swim across its path.
The shark is gone.
Each extra year at sea brings more growth, and more risk: perhaps half of fish survive each later year. Jacks avoid this by returning early.
A crowded year at sea. Pink salmon are abundant every other year, and sockeye grow less when they compete for food.
Weeks later, farther out. Another patch of food, and something large is hunting here too.
Feeding near the surface. Seals and sea lions hunt salmon throughout their years at sea.
Bubbles and a dark shape: a seal. It lunges at where you are going, so turn hard as it comes.
The seal is gone.
Pink salmon everywhere, all after the same food. Get to it first.
A lean season: less food for every fish.
Months pass. Deeper water, and something fast below.
The first autumn at sea.
For a male, this is thought to be when his path is set. His genes, and how fast he has grown, decide whether he matures early.

when: At the start of the stage
line: Coming home from the open sea. Nearing the coast, the salmon stops eating and lives on what it has stored.
The fat bar is all the fuel left for this life. Bursting burns it fast.
Small enough to slip through the mesh. Gillnets catch many returning sockeye, especially the larger males whose heads and teeth tangle, but jacks often slip through.
Past the nets. Find the river mouth that smells like home.
A shadow and a splash at the bank: a bear. Shallow riffles are where bears fish. Wait in a pool, or cross deep and fast.
Reserves are running low. Rest in the slower water near the banks.
The scent is fading. This branch is not home: back out and try the other.

when: At the end of the stage
line: The scent is unmistakable. Home.
In the home river.
A warm, low-water year. Heat stress and low oxygen kill fish before they spawn. Rest in the deeper, cooler pools.
At sea, salmon navigate by the Earth's magnetic field. Feel for it: faint shimmering marks appear ahead when you are on the track. If they fade, sweep side to side until you find them again.
The pull has faded. You've drifted off the track. Sweep across until the shimmer returns.
The coast. This doesn't feel like the right mouth. Overshooting is one of the commonest mistakes; turn back along the shore.
This river doesn't smell like home. Salmon test a river and back out when it is wrong. Turn around.
The smell of home. This is the river.
A flash in the pool: an angler's lure swinging across the current. Give it a wide berth.
Hooked! Burst again and again to tear free before the line wins.
Free. The hook tore loose, but the fight cost precious fat.

when: At the start of the stage
line: The spawning grounds.
Judge the gravel by its cobble: too coarse is hard to dig, too fine and the eggs get less oxygen. Dig the redd, wait over it for a male, then cover the eggs. Drive off rival females with a burst.
Stay beside the female. When a rival comes, ram him side-on with a burst before he reaches her. Fights are quick, and size usually wins.
You are too small to fight. Settle into a hiding spot under the bank. When the big males clash, dart in beside the female.
Digging. Sweeps of the tail lift the gravel and the current carries the fine silt away.
This spot is no good. Look for gravel of medium cobble.
Another female wants this spot. Charge her with a burst.
A rival male is moving in. Ram him side-on with a burst before he reaches her.
Driven off.
A rival dug into your redd.
A rival reached the female while you were away.
The male joins you over the redd. The eggs are laid and fertilized.
The female releases her eggs and you fertilize them.
The big males are fighting. Now!
In and out before the guard noticed. Sneakers can fertilize some of the eggs, though usually fewer than a guarding male.
The guarding male drove you off. Wait for an opening.
Coarse cobble. It is hard work to dig, and the redd will be poor.
Fine gravel. Easy to dig, but the eggs will get less oxygen.
Side-on, mouth open: he gave way. Size usually wins, but timing and position helped.
He gave way.
He was bigger, and you were driven off. Hit rivals side-on, before they reach her.
A bear wades into the shallows. Bears take the biggest males first, then large females, and small jacks last. Watch for its shadow.
The bear took the guarding male.
Too many jacks, too few hiding spots. They fight each other for the cover under the bank.
Another jack holds this hiding spot. Charge him out with a burst, or find another.
You pushed him out of the spot.
Another jack pushed you out of your hiding spot.
Another jack got there first.
A small creek: shallow water and undercut banks. Bears catch fish most easily in creeks, and the bank cover gives jacks places to hide.
A river: deeper, faster water over coarse gravel. River sockeye are larger and deeper-bodied than creek fish, and bears find them harder to catch.
A lake beach: still water along the shore. Beach spawners are the largest and deepest-bodied sockeye. Bears catch fish less easily here than in creeks, and there are few places for jacks to hide.
You are too small to fight. Hide behind a boulder, the only cover on the beach. When the big males clash, dart in beside the female.
The redd is dug. Stay over it and wait for a male.
A male has come to court you. He stays close while you dig.
Two males fight beside your redd. Fights are quick and mostly settled by size, and you will spawn with the winner.
The redd is ready, but no male is beside it. Wait over it.
Now cover the eggs: sweep gravel over them with your tail over the redd.
The eggs are covered. Guard the redd against other females for as long as your strength lasts.
Another female dug into your redd, and some of your eggs were dug up. Drive rivals off with a burst.
Your strength is fading, and here it will not come back. After weeks on the spawning grounds, salmon turn sluggish and ragged.
Your strength is gone. You guarded the redd for as long as you could. Females live several weeks after spawning, rarely more than a month.
Your strength is gone. Like other Pacific salmon, a sockeye dies after spawning.
Your strength is gone, and the season is over.
She is ready to spawn. Get beside her, now.
A second female has started to dig farther along the bed. Go to her, or stay with the first. Leaving costs strength and leaves you more exposed to bears.
You leave her to look for another female.
You stay near her.
The second female releases her eggs and you fertilize them.
She spawned with another male before you reached her.
Many jacks on the grounds this year: more of them compete for every opening, and each sneak is worth less.
Few jacks on the grounds this year: less competition for the openings, and each sneak is worth more.
The yolk ran out before the alevin left the gravel. An alevin has to swim up and start feeding before its stored food is gone.
Washed out. A surge of water tore the alevin from the gravel. High flows that scour the gravel kill many eggs and alevin before they ever emerge.
Taken by a Dolly Varden. Trout and Dolly Varden are the main predators of fry in the lake.
Taken by a diving bird. Smolts near the surface are easy targets for mergansers and gulls.
Taken by an orca.
Taken by a char at the lake outlet. Larger fish gather where the smolts leave the lake.
Taken by a merganser. These diving ducks chase smolts underwater.
Taken by a seal. Seals gather at river mouths when the smolts run, and hunt salmon throughout their years at sea.
Caught in a gillnet. The fish swims in, its head and teeth tangle, and it cannot back out. Larger males are caught most.
Taken by a bear. Bears feed most easily in shallow creeks. They take males first, then large females.
Exhausted. Returning salmon do not eat, and this one ran out of stored energy before reaching home.
Spawning failed. The season ended before this fish could spawn.
Lost at sea during a later year: orcas, salmon sharks or seals. Perhaps half of fish survive each extra year. Jacks, returning after one year, skip this risk.
Taken by a salmon shark.
Landed by an angler. Sport fishing takes returning salmon in the rivers, as the commercial nets do on the approach.

when: After spawning, as the life ends
line: Like other Pacific salmon, a sockeye dies after spawning.

when: After spawning, as the life ends
line: Its body feeds the stream, the insects, the bears and the trees along the bank.

when: After spawning, as the life ends
line: Under the gravel, the next generation is already growing.

when: After spawning, as the life ends
line: Spent, she guards the redd for as long as she can. Females live a few weeks after spawning, rarely more than a month.

when: After spawning, as the life ends
line: Spawned out, he grows sluggish and ragged on the grounds.

when: After spawning, as the life ends
line: The body settles among the stones and slowly breaks down.

when: After spawning, as the life ends
line: Autumn turns to winter, and winter to spring.
